tips.text: The five steps to lean: define value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, pursue perfection. Then start over — it’s a loop, not a checklist, because every improvement exposes the next problem that was hidden underneath it.
Start every improvement from customer value: what quality, price, and delivery is your customer actually paying for? Every change is measured against that.
You cannot improve what you cannot see. Mapping your value stream — and getting live data onto it — is always the first step.
Lean is best learned at the genba — “the actual place”. Walk your floor with the live map in hand and keep your eyes open for waste.
Improve in small steps — the Japanese call it kata. A tiny change whose effect you can watch beats a big redesign whose effects you can’t untangle.
Becoming lean involves everyone — from the line worker to sales. The best person to improve a station’s daily work is the person who runs it.
When you can’t make the obvious improvement, don’t give up — optimize your second choices. The sum of small changes wins in the long run.

A change that speeds up your station can still slow down the line, because stations are coupled: your extra output is simply the next station’s growing queue. Always check what an improvement does one station up- and downstream.
Toyota’s “true north”: the closer you get to optimal, the less rules of thumb help — and the harder you must look at your own data.
What looks like a collection of lean rules is really a set of trade-offs. Speed vs. energy, inventory vs. resilience — knowing your goal decides them.
Memorize the seven wastes as TIMWOOD: Transport, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Over-processing, Overproduction, Defects.
Transport is the easiest waste to spot and often the cheapest to fix — distance is a tax you pay again on every single lot, forever. Store what a station needs as close to it as possible.
Frequently used items belong in the closest stations; rarely used ones can live far away. Sort by frequency of use, not by category.
Your stations are drawn to scale on the floor plan — so the transport statistic is real meters. Rearrange the floor and watch the meters fall.
WIP costs you twice: capital and labor already invested, plus the sale it isn’t yet. Cut work-in-process before adding capacity.
A pile of WIP in front of a station is your bottleneck introducing itself. The heatmap shows it in red.
Inventory hides problems by buffering them. Lowering WIP feels risky — but it exposes the issues you actually need to fix.
Fewer part variants means less stock, better storage stations, and easier handling. Simplify the product to simplify the floor.
Motion is everything a body does — reaching, bending, turning. It always costs time and sometimes health. Level surfaces, closer tools, less strain.
Watch a task like you’d watch video footage: where do hands travel? A workbench aligned with the machine can erase a thousand turns a week.
Waiting is the most visible enemy of flow. Record cycle times per station — the numbers tell you where the line is out of balance.
A line is only as fast as its slowest station. Speeding up any other station produces inventory, not output.
Over-processing is work the customer never asked for: polishing what no one sees, treating every variant alike because routing is hard.

Overproduction is making more, or sooner, than is ordered — in the strictest reading, everything not yet sold. A pull cap prevents it mechanically: nothing new may start until something finished leaves.

“Maximize machine utilization” is how overproduction sneaks in: a machine kept busy beyond the pace of customer demand isn’t productive, it’s converting money into inventory. Machines exist to serve demand’s beat, not the other way around.
The later a defect is found, the more added value is scrapped with it. Check quality at the station, not just at the end.
WIP amplifies defects: a systematic error fills the whole buffer before quality control sees the first bad part. Less WIP = earlier detection.
Waste almost always looks necessary. It only becomes visible when you imagine a better way — that’s why fresh eyes on a genba walk find so much.
Sometimes adding waste in one category removes more in another: slowing a station down (waiting) can reduce defects and overproduction.
An eighth waste: over-qualification. If a task could be done with simpler skills or tools, the surplus is waste too.
“Pull” means a hard cap on WIP: downstream consumption triggers upstream work. Everything else — however busy it looks — is push.
Your lot cards are Kanban cards. Limit how many circulate and you’ve built a pull system — the cap is the whole trick.
Create orders by pulling from the end of the line. Pulling at an intermediate station builds WIP that still has to travel — Taktline warns you for a reason.
Push and pull produce at the same rate — the slowest station decides both. Pull just gets there with a fraction of the WIP, lead time, and rework.
A pull system is a speed limit on the highway: individuals grumble, everyone arrives sooner.

Right-size your kanban count: one card per station approximates single-piece flow, and every extra card is one more lot of WIP standing in line — by Little’s law, more lead time. Add cards only where variability genuinely needs a buffer.

Batch sizes of one sound extreme, but the arithmetic is plain: in a batch of ten, each part spends nine tenths of its life waiting for its batchmates. Every batch-size reduction cuts lead time, space, and rework — move that way in steps.
Little’s law: lead time ≈ WIP ÷ production rate. Halve the WIP in your line and lead time halves — without anyone working faster.
Three levers shorten lead time: remove waste from the process, raise the bottleneck’s rate, and cut WIP with pull. Work them in that order.

Takt time = available time ÷ customer demand — the beat your line must hold to meet demand exactly. Producing to takt is itself a pull system: the beat admits work at the rate the customer consumes it, no faster. A line is balanced when every station’s cycle time sits close to takt.

Three different numbers, constantly confused. Takt time is the beat you need (available time ÷ demand) — a target you set. Cycle time is how long the work actually takes — what Start/Stop measures. Line cycle time is how often a piece really leaves. Cycle time under takt but line cycle time over it means the work is fine and the flow is not.

The gap between cycle time and line cycle time is your waste, in seconds. If a station works a piece in 2 minutes but only ships one every 9, the missing 7 are queueing, blocking or transport — speeding up the operator wins nothing.

The one pass/fail test on the whole board: line cycle time ≤ takt time. If demand needs a unit every 4 minutes and pieces really leave every 3, you are meeting it; if they leave every 5, you are falling a unit behind every 20 minutes, whatever the cycle times say. Check this before anything else — a line can hit every station’s cycle-time target and still miss demand, because cycle time measures the work and takt measures the promise.

When cycle time is far below line cycle time, the work is not the problem — the flow is. A station that fills a piece in 2 minutes but only releases one every 20 is idle 90% of the time: starved from upstream, blocked downstream, or waiting on transport. That ratio is the cheapest improvement in the plant, because you are buying back time you are already paying for.

Chase a cycle/line-cycle gap in this order: upstream first (is the station starved?), then downstream (is it blocked by a full queue?), then transport and changeover. The station showing the gap is rarely the station causing it — which is why “work faster” is almost always the wrong instruction.

When a station’s cycle time exceeds takt, no amount of flow improvement saves you: the work itself is slower than demand. That is a capacity decision — a second operator, a parallel station, a faster process, or fewer orders — not something a better queue can fix. Cycle time above takt is the one problem you cannot organise your way out of.

Takt is not a constant. Recompute it whenever demand or the shift pattern changes: the same line running one shift instead of two has half the available time and therefore half the takt. A takt set once and forgotten is a target measured against last quarter’s order book.

Quote delivery dates from line cycle time, not cycle time. Cycle time is the flattering number — it counts only the minutes someone was actually working, and every hour a lot spent queueing is still an hour your customer waited.
Balance to demand, not to capacity. A station running faster than takt — the pace customer demand sets — isn’t being productive; it’s stacking inventory in front of the next station.
To balance a line: lift the slowest station with lean improvements, slow the fastest only if it saves real money, and split or merge stations when gaps stay wide.

OEE — Overall Equipment Effectiveness, actual output ÷ theoretical maximum — means nothing as a single number, because “theoretical maximum” is defined differently everywhere. It’s the change that talks: a sudden drop says “look here” — downtime, starvation, or quality.
A very high OEE (a station running near its maximum output) is a warning, not a trophy: a station at capacity has no slack, so work queues in front of it — you’re looking at your bottleneck.

A station can only run when its upstream neighbor feeds it — so a low OEE downstream usually indicts the station before it, not the idle one. Never judge equipment effectiveness in isolation; read the whole line.

Don’t set OEE as a target: people will hit it by keeping machines busy making parts nobody ordered — utilization up, overproduction up. Use OEE to locate problems, and optimize toward customer value instead.
Digitize the whole process before digitizing one machine: data without an order attached is hard to turn into customer value.
Lean first, then automate. Layout and flow improvements are free — and they define what a robot must actually do before you buy one.
A machine that saves labor but disrupts flow is a net loss. Judge equipment by its effect on the value stream, not its spec sheet.
Real-time data turns weeks of clipboard studies into hours: watch cycle time, OEE, and the heatmap respond the same day you change something.
5S: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. A workplace where everything has a visible home makes waste — and missing tools — obvious at a glance.
Outline tool positions with shadow boards or tape. If a tool is missing you see it in one second, not after ten minutes of searching.
SMED — single-minute exchange of die: split every changeover into “external” work you can do while the machine runs and “internal” work you can’t. Then move steps from internal to external.
Faster changeovers don’t just save time — they make small batches economical. Cut the changeover in half and you can halve the batch, the WIP, and the lead time.
Poka-yoke — mistake-proofing: design the step so the error is impossible, not just discouraged. A connector that only fits one way beats a warning label every time.
Checklists are the cheapest poka-yoke. Put the check into the lot card’s fields so the operator confirms it where the work happens.
Jidoka: stop the line when something is wrong, immediately. One stopped station is cheap; a buffer full of defective parts is not.

Empower every operator to halt work and flag a problem — the andon principle. Root-cause analysis (your five whys) is fastest while the evidence is still warm; wait a shift and the trail is cold, the WIP pile contaminated.

Heijunka — level the mix: alternate small batches of A, B, C instead of a week of each. Customers order a mix, and an even mix removes the demand spikes (mura) that would otherwise force big buffers everywhere — leveling is what makes a tight pull cap livable.
Standard work is the baseline of improvement: without a documented “current best way”, you can’t tell whether a change helped or the day was just lucky.
Write the standard with the people who do the work — then improve the standard, not the person.
Muda is waste, mura is unevenness, muri is overburden. Uneven flow creates overburden, and overburden creates waste — level first, then optimize.

PDCA — Plan, Do, Check, Act — is the engine inside kata, genba walks, and the five lean steps: they’re all the same improvement loop at different scales. Every change is an experiment, so decide before you act which number should move; most efforts die at “Check” because nobody ever looks.

Ask “why” five times to get behind the symptom: machine stopped → fuse blew → bearing seized → no lubrication → no maintenance plan. Fixing the fuse cures today; fixing the plan cures the whole class of failures. This is the root-cause drill inside every PDCA “Check”.

The “theory of constraints” is the pull idea in different words: one station — the bottleneck — sets your whole line’s output, so release new work only at the pace that station consumes it. TOC does it with a schedule (“drum-buffer-rope”), kanban does it with cards; both are WIP caps.

Protect the bottleneck: an hour lost there is an hour lost for the whole plant, because no other station can make up for it. Give it a small deliberate buffer so it never starves — and remember that an hour “saved” anywhere else doesn’t add output, it just piles WIP in front of the bottleneck.
A visitor should understand the state of your floor in three minutes without asking anyone. If they can’t, add visual management — boards, colors, markings.
Metrics belong where the work happens, not in a monthly PDF. A number nobody sees daily changes nobody’s behavior.
Quality at the source: the operator checks their own output before passing it on. Ten seconds of self-check saves ten minutes of downstream rework.

Goodhart’s law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring — people optimize the number, not the thing it stood for. Chase OEE and you get overproduction; chase ship-dates alone and you get defects. Reward improvement of the system, not the number.
Trace one product’s actual path on a floor plan — the “spaghetti diagram”. The tangles you see are transport and motion waste you can delete with layout alone.
Store parts at the point of use, in the orientation they’re used, at the height they’re used. Every re-grip and re-turn is motion waste.
U-shaped cells put the first and last step side by side: one operator can run the whole loop, and imbalances become visible immediately.
Lean’s second pillar is respect for people. Nobody knows a station’s waste better than the person who runs it eight hours a day — ask them first.
Cross-train deliberately and keep a visible skill matrix. Multi-skilled teams absorb absences and demand spikes without breaking flow.
A five-minute daily huddle at the board beats an hour-long weekly meeting in a conference room. Decide at the genba, with the data in view.

Total productive maintenance: small daily care by the operator — clean, inspect, lubricate — prevents big unplanned stops. Planned maintenance pauses one station on your schedule; a breakdown pauses the whole line on the machine’s schedule.

FIFO — first in, first out: work the oldest lot first. When lots overtake each other, some wait unpredictably long (your quoted lead time becomes a lie) and the time window for tracing a defect’s cause gets scrambled. Deviate only by a deliberate priority rule.
The 80/20 rule holds on the shop floor: a few defect types cause most rework, a few products cause most changeovers. Count first, then fix the tallest bar.
Mount a tablet with the Operator view at each station. Timing happens as a side effect of working — and your takt and OEE statistics build themselves.
Print lot labels and scan to advance: one barcode scan moves the lot and timestamps the transport. No screen, no typing, no forgotten bookings.
Set your real work hours in Settings → Global. OEE measured against a 24/7 clock punishes you for sleeping — measure against the hours you actually run.
A lot code is a traceability thread: released from an order it carries the order’s reference, and every split piece keeps it. Quote it in every quality conversation.
At a merge station, check the feeding-stations panel before walking: it shows what’s finished upstream, and one tap jumps you there to fetch it.
Watch the Lots board for a week before changing anything. The column that’s always full is your real bottleneck — it is rarely the one everyone suspects.
Let orders drive the floor: connect your shop or ERP and each sale releases exactly the lots it needs — pull all the way from the customer.

concepts.title: Little's law
concepts.claim: Halve the work on your floor and lead time halves — with nobody working faster.
concepts.formula: lead time = products in process ÷ throughput
concepts.body: It holds for any stable system, whatever the layout, scheduling or luck. Sixty products on the floor and twenty leaving a day means three days inside — full stop. It also works backwards as a lie detector: check a promised lead time against WIP and throughput in one division.

concepts.title: Kingman's formula
concepts.claim: At 90% utilisation a product waits nine times its own work time. At 95%, nineteen.
concepts.body: The utilisation term is hyperbolic, so queue time runs away smoothly with no warning knee — which is why busy factories are slow ones. The variability term multiplies the same queue at the same load, so irregular arrivals inflate the wait even on a half-loaded station. Two independent levers, and "keep everyone busy" attacks neither.

concepts.title: Balance efficiency
concepts.claim: A 40-minute station beside a 25-minute one buys you 15 minutes of waiting per product — every product, forever.
concepts.formula: E = Σ work content ÷ (n × slowest station)
concepts.body: Every station is paced by the slowest, so the gap between a station and the slowest one is structural idle time: designed in, paid every cycle, however well anyone works. Move work from the slow station to the fast one, or merge two short ones, and you recover it without anyone hurrying.

concepts.title: Flow efficiency
concepts.claim: If a product takes 3 hours of work and 3 weeks to arrive, doubling the speed of every machine improves delivery by 1%.
concepts.formula: flow efficiency = value-added time ÷ lead time
concepts.body: Real processes land between 1% and 5%. The leverage is entirely in the waiting, which is why cutting WIP beats buying speed almost everywhere — and why this and Kingman are the same argument from two directions.

concepts.title: Common cause and special cause
concepts.claim: Adjusting a process for every wobble makes it worse. Most "corrective action" is tampering.
concepts.body: Shewhart's split: common-cause variation is inherent to the system and can only be reduced by changing the system; special-cause variation has a findable external origin. Inside the limits, do not react. A station bouncing between 58% and 66% OEE has a system to improve; one that drops to 30% on Tuesdays has an event to find.

concepts.title: Matched sets
concepts.claim: 90% of parts finished can still mean zero assemblies possible.
concepts.body: An assembly needs all of its precursors, so a kit completes at its slowest member, not its average. Part-level completion percentages mislead badly in assembly shops, and releasing partial kits just moves inventory nearer the point where it still cannot be used. Buffer in complete kits, never in bins of whichever part is easiest to make.

concepts.title: Monuments
concepts.claim: The spreadsheet that justifies the big machine almost never prices the queue it creates.
concepts.body: A monument is a large, fixed, high-capacity machine the flow has to route around: the furnace, the plating line, the big paint booth. It forces batching, breaks one-piece flow, and creates contention between product families that would otherwise never meet — and it becomes a permanent constraint, because you cannot buy half a second one.

concepts.title: Theory of constraints
concepts.claim: An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole plant. An hour saved anywhere else is a mirage.
concepts.body: Every line has exactly one slowest point at a time, and the system's throughput is that point's throughput. Identify it, exploit it so it never waits, subordinate everything else to its pace, elevate it only once exploitation is exhausted — then repeat, because fixing one constraint reveals the next.

concepts.title: 5S
concepts.claim: If a missing tool is not obvious in one second, your workplace is hiding it from you.
concepts.body: Sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain. The test is not whether the floor looks tidy — it is whether an absence is visible. A shadow board shows a missing spanner instantly; a drawer hides it for ten minutes, every time.

concepts.title: Standard work
concepts.claim: Without a documented current best way, you cannot tell whether a change helped or the day was just lucky.
concepts.body: Standard work is the baseline improvement is measured against, which makes it the precondition for improvement rather than the enemy of it. Write it with the people who do the work — then improve the standard, not the person.

concepts.title: Visual management
concepts.claim: A visitor should understand the state of your floor in three minutes without asking anyone.
concepts.body: If they cannot, the information exists only in people’s heads and in a monthly PDF nobody opens. Metrics belong where the work happens: a number nobody sees daily changes nobody’s behaviour.

concepts.title: Spaghetti diagrams
concepts.claim: Trace one product’s actual path on your floor plan. The tangles are waste you can delete with layout alone.
concepts.body: Transport and motion are the two wastes you can remove without changing how anyone works — you move the benches instead. Store parts at the point of use, in the orientation they are used, at the height they are used; every re-grip is motion.

concepts.title: One-piece flow
concepts.claim: In a batch of ten, each part spends nine tenths of its life waiting for its batchmates.
concepts.body: That is the whole argument for small batches, and it is arithmetic rather than philosophy. Every batch-size reduction cuts lead time, floor space and rework — and each one needs a faster changeover to pay for itself, which is why SMED and flow are the same project.

concepts.title: Poka-yoke
concepts.claim: A connector that only fits one way beats a warning label every time.
concepts.body: Mistake-proofing means designing the step so the error is impossible, not discouraged. Training and attention are consumable; a jig that only accepts the part the right way round is not. Checklists are the cheapest version.

concepts.title: Jidoka
concepts.claim: One stopped station is cheap. A buffer full of defective parts is not.
concepts.body: Stop the line when something is wrong, immediately, and give every operator the authority to do it. Root-cause analysis is fastest while the evidence is warm — wait a shift and the trail is cold and the WIP pile is contaminated.

concepts.title: Quality at the source
concepts.claim: The later a defect is found, the more added value is scrapped with it.
concepts.body: Ten seconds of self-check at the station saves ten minutes of downstream rework — and WIP amplifies the arithmetic, because a systematic error fills the whole buffer before final inspection sees the first bad part. Less WIP, earlier detection.

concepts.title: SMED
concepts.claim: Halve the changeover and you can halve the batch, the WIP and the lead time.
concepts.body: Split every changeover into external work you can do while the machine runs and internal work you cannot, then move steps from internal to external. Faster changeovers do not just save the changeover — they make small batches economic.

concepts.title: Heijunka
concepts.claim: Customers order a mix. Producing a week of each creates the demand spikes that force buffers everywhere.
concepts.body: Level the mix: alternate small batches of A, B and C instead. Unevenness (mura) is what creates overburden, and overburden is what creates waste — so levelling comes first, and it is what makes a tight pull cap livable.

concepts.title: Total productive maintenance
concepts.claim: Planned maintenance pauses one station on your schedule. A breakdown pauses the line on the machine’s.
concepts.body: Small daily care by the operator — clean, inspect, lubricate — prevents the big unplanned stop. The person who runs the machine every day notices the noise change weeks before the bearing seizes, if they have been asked to listen.

concepts.title: PDCA
concepts.claim: Most improvement efforts die at "Check", because nobody ever looks.
concepts.body: Plan, do, check, act is the engine inside kata, genba walks and the five lean steps — the same loop at different scales. Every change is an experiment, so decide before you act which number should move, and then go and look at it.

concepts.title: Five whys
concepts.claim: Machine stopped → fuse blew → bearing seized → no lubrication → no maintenance plan. Fixing the fuse cures today.
concepts.body: Ask why five times to get behind the symptom. Fixing the plan cures the whole class of failures; fixing the fuse means meeting the same fault again next quarter, wearing a different mask.

concepts.title: Pareto
concepts.claim: A few defect types cause most of your rework. Count first, then fix the tallest bar.
concepts.body: The 80/20 rule holds on a shop floor as reliably as anywhere: a few products cause most changeovers, a few causes most scrap. Counting is cheap and it stops you improving the thing that happens to be annoying rather than expensive.

concepts.title: Respect for people
concepts.claim: Nobody knows a station’s waste better than the person who runs it eight hours a day.
concepts.body: Lean’s second pillar, and the one most often skipped. Ask them first; write the standard with them; cross-train deliberately and keep the skill matrix visible. A five-minute daily huddle at the board beats an hour in a conference room.
